title: Interface Force Field
subtitle: A beginner’s guide to simulating where molecules meet solid materials
author: Sean Florez

slides.title: Interface Force Field
slides.alt: A short peptide lying on a platinum surface, surrounded by water molecules.
notes: How can a computer tell us which face of a crystal a molecule will stick to, and why should we believe its answer? We build the tools one at a time, from a single pair of atoms up to whole surfaces in water, and then look at three published studies where the Interface Force Field, or IFF, was compared with experiments.
The picture is a peptide called S7 lying on platinum in water. It comes back in the first example and at the end.

The crystal structures come from the Crystallography Open Database or from published lattice sizes, and the surfaces were built from them with ASE and the molecules with RDKit, all open software. The pictures of molecules on surfaces are illustrations, arranged to show the idea rather than taken from a simulation. Every result quoted comes from the cited papers and was not rerun here. Besides the worked arithmetic, the one calculation made for this presentation is the electron cloud of a water molecule, and it only draws a picture.
slides.lede: The picture shows a peptide, a short chain of amino acids, lying on a platinum surface in water. This guide shows how a computer can work out where molecules like this stick, starting from a single pair of atoms.

slides.title: Can one amino acid change the shape of a metal crystal?
slides.takeaway: A crystal’s shape is set by which faces molecules stick to, since those faces grow slowest and end up covering it. So why does F stick to the triangular faces?
slides.alt: Two short peptides, TLT and TFT, differ only in their middle amino acid. With TLT platinum grows as cubes, whose faces show a square pattern of atoms. With TFT it shifts toward tetrahedra, whose faces show a triangular pattern.
notes: Proteins are chains of amino acids, and a peptide is a short chain. Each amino acid has a one-letter code. Here T is threonine, L is leucine and F is phenylalanine, which carries a flat ring of six carbon atoms.

Ruan and colleagues grew platinum crystals in water with each peptide present. With TLT the crystals came out as cubes, whose faces all show a square pattern of atoms. With TFT the crystals shifted toward tetrahedra, whose faces all show a triangular pattern. Chemists call these the {100} and {111} faces.

A crystal grows by adding atoms to its faces. A molecule that sticks to one kind of face slows growth there, so that face ends up covering the crystal. The question is how a simulation could explain why F prefers the triangular face.
slides.lede: A peptide is a short chain of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Ruan and colleagues grew platinum crystals in water with one peptide present. Changing only its middle amino acid from L to F, the one with a flat ring, shifted the crystals from cubes toward tetrahedra, pyramids with four triangular faces.

slides.title: Where molecules stick changes how materials grow and work
slides.lede: The platinum puzzle is one case of a much wider question. Wherever a solid meets water and molecules, what sticks where changes how the material grows and behaves, from tiny metal crystals to bones and cement.
slides.takeaway: If a computer can get these contacts right, ideas can be tested before anything is made, and that is what IFF is built to do.
slides.alt: Four places where what sticks to a surface matters, each with a short caption. Catalysts, shown by a platinum cube and a platinum tetrahedron. Medicine, shown by a gold rod. Bones and teeth, shown by the peptide SVSVGGK on hydroxyapatite, the mineral in bone. Cement, shown by two broken faces of a cement grain with molecules of a grinding additive between them.
notes: The platinum question is one case of a wider one. Metal nanocrystals are used as catalysts, which speed up chemical reactions, and in medicine, for example gold nanorods for photothermal cancer therapy, in which the rods turn light into heat. Geada and colleagues point out that the growth and shape of such crystals, and how well they work as catalysts, as sensors or in the body, are affected by what happens right at the metal surface.

Hydroxyapatite is the mineral in bones and teeth. Lin and Heinz note that conditions such as osteoporosis, tooth decay and calcium build-up in the arteries of the heart affect the quality of life of billions of people. Proteins and other molecules from the body steer how the mineral grows, and these contacts are hard to study in the lab at the scale of 1 to 100 nanometres. As an example, Lin and Heinz simulated SVSVGGK, a peptide known to bind the mineral strongly, on its flat basal face.

Making cement means grinding hard lumps called clinker into a fine powder, a central step and a major cost. A patent on grinding additives describes how small amounts of molecules such as amino alcohols cut the grinding time and energy sharply and stop the powder clumping. Mishra, Flatt and Heinz simulated such additives, including triethanolamine, between two broken faces of tricalcium silicate, a main ingredient of cement. Their result is in the notes for the last slide.
In every case the question is the one from platinum, which molecules stick to which face and how strongly. A model that answers it on a computer lets researchers try ideas before anything is made.
The four pictures use real crystal structures and molecules, but their arrangements are illustrations, not simulation results.

slides.kicker: Why IFF exists · Models that do not fit
slides.title: Models built separately do not fit together
slides.takeaway: The Interface Force Field (IFF) writes the metal in the molecules’ equations, then tunes it to measured surfaces.
slides.alt: Left, a metal model and a molecular model built separately, with no shared rule between them and metal surface energies up to 50% too low. Right, the Interface Force Field writes the metal in the molecules’ equations, so the pairs between them follow the same rules, within 5% of measured surface and water-interface energies.
notes: To simulate a peptide on platinum in water, the computer needs rules for three sets of interactions. Platinum atoms hold the solid together. Water molecules and the peptide interact with each other. And every platinum atom interacts with every nearby atom of water and peptide, and this third set decides which crystal face the peptide sticks to.

Good rules for the first two sets already existed, but separately. Metal models were built to describe metals, and molecular models were built to describe water and proteins. The third set needs both sides described in the same terms.

A popular metal model, the embedded-atom method, uses equations of its own, while protein models such as CHARMM and AMBER use different ones. Nothing in either says how a metal atom should feel a water molecule. Kanhaiya and colleagues also report that metal-only models of this kind give surface energies up to about 50% too low.

IFF describes the metal with the same simple equation the molecular models already use between atoms that are not bonded, the Lennard-Jones curve we meet shortly. Its two numbers per metal are tuned so the simulated metal has the measured density and surface energy, and the metal–molecule pairs then follow from the same rules. For ten metals, Kanhaiya and colleagues report agreement with experiment within 0.1 to 5% for lattice size, surface energy, water interface energy and binding of organic molecules.
slides.lede: To simulate a peptide on platinum in water, a computer needs rules for how every pair of atoms pulls or pushes. Good rules existed for metals and for molecules, but each was written in its own equations, so nothing said how a metal atom should feel a water molecule.

slides.title: IFF puts solids and molecules in one compatible model
slides.alt: Four kinds of solid that IFF describes, metals, silica, hydroxyapatite and cement, above three kinds of molecule it is combined with, water, peptides and proteins, and polymers.
notes: A force-field family is a complete set of rules and numbers for one kind of chemistry, such as AMBER, CHARMM and OPLS-AA for proteins and organic molecules, or PCFF for polymers. IFF adds solids, such as metals, silica, minerals and cement, written in the same style as those families so the two can be used together.

The surfaces are built to match the real ones, including the OH groups on silica and the way a mineral surface changes with acidity. One simulation can then hold a solid, water and a molecule together, and its results can be compared with experiments.

IFF supplies compatible interaction equations and material parameters so a classical simulation can describe a solid together with water, polymers or biological molecules. It addresses inconsistent material/surface descriptions and the difficulty of combining separately developed models, allowing supported interface structures, binding and energies to be calculated and compared with experiments.
slides.lede: IFF covers solids such as metals, silica, the mineral in bone and teeth, and cement. Each is written in the same style as the standard models for water, proteins and polymers, the long chains in plastics, and its surfaces are built to match real ones.
slides.takeaway: So one simulation can hold a solid, water and molecules together, and its results can be checked against experiments.

slides.title: A force field replaces the electron cloud with simple rules
slides.takeaway: The catch is that the numbers in these rules have to be tuned and checked against experiments.
slides.alt: A water molecule shown two ways. Left, its electron cloud computed with quantum chemistry around one oxygen and two hydrogen nuclei. Right, the same molecule as balls joined by springs, with a small negative charge on the oxygen and small positive charges on the hydrogens.
notes: Every atom has a small, heavy nucleus made of protons and, in most atoms, neutrons, surrounded by a cloud of electrons. Where atoms sit and how they hold together is decided by these electrons.

Quantum chemistry computes the electron cloud directly. The most common method is density functional theory, or DFT, which uses an approximate formula called a functional to describe how electrons affect each other. It is accurate but slow, so it is usually limited to hundreds or a few thousand atoms.

A force field skips the electrons. Atoms become balls, bonds become springs, and each atom carries a fixed partial charge, a fraction of an electron’s charge, written δ− or δ+. In water the oxygen pulls electrons towards itself, so it is slightly negative and the hydrogens slightly positive.

Machine-learned force fields sit in between. A model such as MACE or AI²BMD is trained to reproduce quantum results on many example structures, and it is reliable only for structures like the ones it was trained on. A classical force field such as IFF uses fixed rules, so it is the fastest of these methods and reaches millions of atoms, but a standard one never breaks or forms bonds. It suits questions about surfaces, binding and water, where bonds stay intact.
The cloud on the left is a real calculation of one water molecule, made with the PySCF program and the PBE functional. The balls and springs on the right are a drawing of the same molecule.
slides.lede: Atoms are held together by their electrons. Quantum chemistry computes the electron cloud directly, which is accurate but slow, so it handles hundreds or a few thousand atoms. A force field replaces the cloud with balls, springs and small fixed charges, which is fast enough for millions.

slides.kicker: Molecular mechanics · Five kinds of terms
slides.title: The energy is a sum of five kinds of terms
slides.takeaway: The first three keep each molecule in shape. Van der Waals and charges also act between molecules and solids, so they decide what sticks where.
slides.alt: Five panels show the same ethanol molecule next to a water molecule, each highlighting only the atoms in one term. 1, bond stretch, an arrow along the O–H bond. 2, angle bend, an arc across the C–O–H angle. 3, twist, an arrow turning the three end hydrogens around the C–C bond. 4, van der Waals, a dashed line from an ethanol hydrogen to a water hydrogen. 5, charges, a dashed line from the δ+ hydrogen of ethanol’s OH group to the δ− oxygen of water. Below, the energy is the five terms added up over every bond, angle, twist and pair of atoms.
notes: Molecular mechanics adds up the energy of a whole system from simple pieces. Bond stretching, angle bending and twisting act along the chemical bonds inside a molecule. Van der Waals and charge interactions act between atoms that are not bonded to each other, including atoms in different molecules, and between a molecule and a solid.

Bonds and angles act like springs. A bond has a natural length, and stretching or squeezing it costs energy that grows with the square of the change, E = k (r − r₀)², so twice the stretch costs four times the energy. An angle works the same way, E = k (θ − θ₀)². Water’s O–H bond rests at about 0.96 ångström, where one ångström is a ten-billionth of a metre, and its H–O–H angle rests at about 104.5 degrees. Each family tunes the stiffness k so that molecules vibrate at their measured frequencies. The springs never break, so a standard force field cannot describe chemical reactions, in which bonds form or break.

Twisting around a bond has favourite angles. Ethane is two carbon atoms, each carrying three hydrogens. Looking along the bond between the carbons, the back hydrogens can sit between the front ones, called staggered, or behind them, called eclipsed, which costs a little more energy. The energy repeats every 120°, and a force field describes it with a smooth wave, E = k [1 + cos(nφ − δ)], where φ is the twist angle, n is the number of repeats in a full turn, three for ethane, and δ shifts where the lowest points fall. The height k is tuned to measurements or to quantum chemistry. Twisting terms like this decide how flexible molecules such as peptides and polymers fold and bend.

Each force-field family writes these pieces in its own way and with its own numbers. Some write the spring energy with a factor of one half and some leave it out, so stiffness numbers cannot be copied from one family into another without checking. Some, such as PCFF, add extra terms that couple stretching and bending and use a softer van der Waals curve, but all of them build the energy from these five pieces. Families also differ in how they treat atoms close together in one molecule. Pairs joined by one or two bonds are usually left out of the van der Waals and charge sums, and pairs three bonds apart are counted in full or scaled down, depending on the family.

A simulation then moves the atoms. Molecular dynamics adds up the force on every atom, moves every atom a tiny step according to those forces, and repeats. Each step is typically one femtosecond, a millionth of a billionth of a second, so a million steps make one nanosecond. Averages over many steps give measurable quantities such as density, energy or binding. Energy minimization, a related method, skips the motion and moves the atoms straight downhill to the nearest low-energy arrangement.
slides.lede: A force field works out the energy of a group of atoms by adding up five simple kinds of terms. Here they act on a real ethanol molecule next to a water molecule. Bonds stretch, angles bend and groups twist around bonds, while atoms that are not bonded feel van der Waals forces and the pull or push of their charges.

slides.kicker: Van der Waals · The Lennard-Jones curve
slides.title: Two atoms attract until they get too close
slides.lede: Even neutral atoms pull on each other weakly, and push apart hard when their electron clouds overlap. The Lennard-Jones curve shows this energy against distance for two rhodium atoms, using IFF’s published numbers. The lowest point is where the pair would rest.
slides.takeaway: The distance of the lowest point, r₀, and the depth of the well, ε, set the whole curve.
slides.alt: The energy of two rhodium atoms against the distance between them. It rises steeply when they are closer than 2.5 Å, has its lowest point of −7.84 kcal/mol at 2.757 Å, and fades towards zero beyond 4 Å, with three pairs of atoms drawn at 2.4, 2.757 and 4.2 Å.
notes: Even neutral atoms attract each other weakly, because their electron clouds flicker and pull on each other. This is the van der Waals attraction. When the atoms get too close, their electron clouds overlap and they push apart strongly.

Energies here are in kilocalories per mole, the energy of one mole of such pairs, about 6 × 10²³ of them. The rhodium curve has its lowest point at r₀ = 2.757 Å with a depth ε of 7.84 kcal/mol. These two numbers were tuned so that simulated rhodium has the measured density and surface energy.
The curve is called 12-6 because its push grows as the twelfth power of one over the distance and its pull as the sixth power. Written with the lowest point, it is E = ε [(r₀/r)¹² − 2 (r₀/r)⁶].

The force on the atoms is the slope of the curve with its sign flipped. At 2.5 Å the energy is still negative, about −2.8 kcal/mol, yet the slope is steep and the atoms push apart with a force of about 54 kcal/mol per ångström. At 3.0 Å the slope is gentle and the atoms pull together with about 7.5. At 2.757 Å the curve is flat and the force is zero. A simulation moves atoms using these forces, so the shape of the curve matters as much as its depth.

Each metal gets its own pair of numbers. In the same study iridium has r₀ = 2.785 Å and ε = 9.20 kcal/mol, calcium 4.025 Å and 3.36, and strontium 4.379 Å and 3.40. Calcium and strontium are larger atoms, so their lowest points sit further out. A deeper well means the atoms hold on to each other more strongly, which goes with a higher surface energy. The study gives values like these for ten metals and for stainless steel.

Pairs of unlike atoms come from a mixing rule. A simulation with 10 kinds of atoms has 55 different pairs, too many to fit one by one, so the rule builds every unlike pair from the two like ones. The rule used here takes the geometric mean, the square root of the product. For rhodium with calcium, r₀ = √(2.757 × 4.025) = 3.331 Å and ε = √(7.84 × 3.36) = 5.13 kcal/mol. Families such as CHARMM and AMBER use the ordinary average for r₀ instead, so the rule must match the family the numbers are used with. This is a worked example of the rule, not a claim about real rhodium–calcium alloys.

The same curve is often written with σ, the distance where the energy crosses zero, which is shorter than r₀ by a factor of 1.1225. Programs such as LAMMPS expect σ. The 2021 paper calls its 2.757 Å σ but means the lowest point, which earlier IFF papers called r₀. If 2.757 Å is typed in as a zero crossing, the lowest point moves out to 3.095 Å, 12% too far. Five cells of rhodium would then measure about 21.3 Å instead of 19.0, and the surface energy would be wrong, all without any error message.

The fix is σ = 2.757 / 1.1225 = 2.456 Å. A force-field file can load without errors and still describe a different material, so after converting, check the curve family and the units the program expects, then compute one pair by hand. Its energy at 2.757 Å should read −7.84 kcal/mol, not 0, and its force should be zero. A 2021 correction to the paper added missing supplementary files and changed none of its tables.

slides.title: Charges reach much further than van der Waals
slides.lede: Atoms in a force field also carry charges. Opposite charges pull together and like charges push apart, and the energy fades only slowly with distance. Here two unit charges in a vacuum, like a sodium and a chloride ion, are drawn on the same axes as the rhodium pair from before.
slides.takeaway: At 10 Å two opposite charges still feel −33 kcal/mol, while the van der Waals pull has all but vanished.
slides.alt: Energy against distance for two opposite unit charges, which pull together with −110.7 kcal/mol at 3 Å and still −33.2 at 10 Å, two like charges, which push apart, and the rhodium van der Waals curve, which is close to zero beyond 4 Å.
notes: Coulomb’s law says the energy of two charges falls off only as one over the distance, E = 332.064 q₁q₂ / r. The number converts the energy to kcal/mol when r is in ångströms and the charges q₁ and q₂ are in elementary charges, the charge of one proton. Two opposite unit charges in a vacuum, such as a sodium ion and a chloride ion, have −110.7 kcal/mol at 3 Å and still −33.2 at 10 Å. The rhodium van der Waals pull at 10 Å is about −0.007.

In water the pull between ions is about 80 times weaker, because water molecules turn so that their opposite partial charge faces each ion, which screens it. A force field does not add this screening by hand. It comes out of the partial charges on the water molecules themselves.

slides.kicker: What IFF does differently · Surface energy
slides.title: IFF tunes each solid to its measured surface energy
slides.lede: Atoms at a surface have lost some neighbours, so making a surface costs energy. Splitting a block makes two new faces, and the energy needed divided by their area is the surface energy. IFF tunes its two rhodium numbers so the simulated block has the measured size and surface energy.
slides.takeaway: Stiffness was not tuned, so it is a real test, and the stretching stiffness comes out 45% low, 209 against 379 GPa.
slides.alt: A block of rhodium pulled apart into two halves, exposing two new faces coloured pink, each of area A. The surface energy is the energy to pull apart divided by 2A, measured at 2.64 ± 0.02 J/m² and computed by IFF at 2.643 J/m².
notes: Atoms at a surface have lost some of their neighbours, so a surface costs energy. Splitting a block makes two new faces, so the surface energy is the energy needed to pull the halves apart divided by twice the area of one face. It is measured in joules per square metre.

The energy of the block is the sum over every pair of atoms in it. Three rhodium atoms at the lowest-energy distance make three pairs, so their total is 3 × (−7.84) = −23.52 kcal/mol. Inside the crystal each atom has 12 nearest neighbours, each 2.689 Å away. That is closer than r₀ because the farther neighbours also pull, squeezing the nearest ones a little closer than a lone pair would sit. In practice a simulation adds up pairs out to a cutoff distance, beyond which the van der Waals pull is too weak to matter.

Rhodium is a face-centred cubic, or fcc, metal. Its repeating cell is a cube 3.803 Å on a side with an atom at each corner and one in the middle of each face. Each corner atom is shared by eight cells and each face atom by two, so one cell holds 8 × ⅛ + 6 × ½ = 4 atoms. Five cells in each direction give 500 atoms, and the simulation box repeats in every direction, called periodic boundaries, so the block behaves like part of an endless crystal. The two rhodium numbers were tuned to give this block its measured size, 19.016 Å along each edge, so that agreement is a calibration rather than a test.

For rhodium’s triangular face the measured surface energy is 2.64 ± 0.02 J/m² and the model gives 2.643. Like the crystal size, this was a tuning target, so it confirms the tuning rather than tests the model. Two small differences remain. The measurements may come from samples with mixed faces and read 1 to 2% high. The simulation gives an energy, while the measurement gives a free energy, which also counts entropy, a measure of how many ways the atoms can move and arrange themselves. The authors estimate that these two differences partly cancel.

Stiffness was not a tuning target, so it tests the model. It is measured in gigapascals, and one gigapascal is about ten thousand times the pressure of the atmosphere. For squeezing from all sides, the bulk modulus, the model gives 258 GPa against a measured 276, 6.5% low. For stretching, Young’s modulus, it gives 209 against 379, and for sliding one layer over another, the shear modulus, 77 against 147. Other measurements give 269 to 271 GPa for squeezing, 319 and 378 for stretching and 150 for shearing.

Curves that act only between pairs of atoms force two of the crystal’s stiffness constants to be equal, and real rhodium does not follow that rule. So the model is good for surfaces and interfaces, but its stiffness is a known weakness.

Force fields such as PCFF, COMPASS and CFF use a softer 9-6 curve, E = ε [2 (r₀/r)⁹ − 3 (r₀/r)⁶], whose push grows as the ninth power instead of the twelfth, while CHARMM, AMBER, OPLS-AA and CVFF use the 12-6 curve. Because the shapes differ, IFF publishes separate rhodium values for each. The 9-6 values are r₀ = 2.807 Å and ε = 6.38 kcal/mol. Both sets reproduce the crystal size and the surface energy, 2.643 J/m², but the 9-6 crystal is softer still, 175 GPa against 276 measured for squeezing. Using 12-6 numbers in a 9-6 force field, or the reverse, gives a different material without any error message.

slides.title: Example 1: The F ring lies flat on platinum’s triangular face
slides.lede: Ruan and colleagues simulated S7, a seven-amino-acid peptide with an F, on both platinum faces in water, using IFF’s early metal model. On the triangular face its flat ring lies down and the peptide sticks. On the square face the ring stands up, and water keeps the surface.
slides.takeaway: What decides the shape is this contrast between the faces, not just how strongly the peptide sticks.
slides.alt: Illustration of the S7 peptide in water on two platinum faces. On the triangular face its phenylalanine ring lies flat and the peptide sticks. On the square face the ring stands up and the peptide does not stick, computed at +3 kcal/mol, so water keeps the surface. In the lab, every peptide version with F grew many tetrahedra, crystals with only triangular faces, and versions without F grew few.
notes: S7 is a seven-amino-acid peptide, SSFPQPN, found by screening many peptides for ones that bind platinum. Ruan and colleagues simulated it on both faces in water with CHARMM-METAL, IFF’s early model for metals, which combines the CHARMM protein model with metal parameters written the same way.

On the triangular face the F ring lies flat, because its six carbons fit the triangular pattern of platinum atoms. On the square face the ring stands up instead, and the computed binding energy of +3 kcal/mol means the peptide does not stick, so water keeps that surface covered.

In the lab, every version of the peptide that contained F grew many tetrahedra, crystals with only triangular faces, and versions without F grew mainly cuboctahedra. One version, S7-G, with F replaced by glycine, G, still binds the triangular face strongly, at about −52 kcal/mol, but it also binds the square face, so it gives few tetrahedra. Versions with tyrosine in place of F lie flat on both faces. What matters is the contrast between the faces. The same idea explains the TLT to TFT switch from the opening.
The pictures are illustrations of these poses, not snapshots from the simulations.

slides.title: Example 2: Water spreads or beads up depending on the silica surface
slides.lede: Silica, the main part of sand and glass, carries OH groups on its surface, and heating drives them off. Water spreads flat on the covered surface and beads up on the heated one. Emami and colleagues simulated water on a silica model for each sample, and the angles came within 3° of the measured ones.
slides.takeaway: The match depends on building each model surface with the same OH density as its real sample.
slides.alt: Illustration of water on two silica surfaces. With OH groups on the surface, the water spreads flat at 0°. With the OH groups removed by heating, the water beads up into a droplet with a 42° contact angle. The simulated angles came within 3° of the measured ones on every surface tested, including two in between.
notes: Heating silica to between 200 and 1000 °C drives off its OH groups. On the fully covered surface water spreads flat, with a contact angle of 0°, and on the most heated surface it beads up at about 42°. The contact angle is the angle between the surface and the edge of a droplet, so a small angle means the water spreads.
Emami and colleagues built silica models with 4.7, 2.35, 1.2 and 0 OH groups per square nanometre to match these samples. The simulated angles came within 3° of the measured ones.

With a standard water model called TIP3P, the model also releases 160 mJ/m² of heat when dry silica with 4.7 OH groups per square nanometre is dipped in water, against 160 ± 5 measured. The paper lists both matches as features of the model, not as independent tests. A 2016 correction to the paper changed only two density plots, not these results.
The droplets are drawn to these angles and are not simulation snapshots.

slides.title: Example 3: Bone mineral changes its surface with pH
slides.lede: Hydroxyapatite, the mineral in bone and teeth, is made of calcium, phosphate and hydroxide. As the water around it turns more acidic, which means a lower pH, hydrogen ions join the surface phosphates and some calcium leaves. Lin and Heinz built a model surface for each pH.
slides.takeaway: The surface a molecule meets depends on pH, so a model must be built for the pH of the experiment.
slides.alt: Three slices of a hydroxyapatite surface. Above pH 14 the bare crystal shows phosphate, calcium and hydroxide. At pH 10 one hydrogen has joined each surface phosphate and some calcium has left. At pH 5 a second hydrogen has joined and more calcium has left. The simulated mineral gives off 619 mJ/m² as water wets it at pH 7, or 533 if all faces count equally, and experiments find 600–700.
notes: Hydroxyapatite is made of calcium ions, phosphate groups and hydroxide ions. pH measures how acidic water is, with 7 neutral and lower numbers more acidic. Protonation means a hydrogen ion, H⁺, attaching to a group such as phosphate.

Lin and Heinz built surface models for different pH. The bare crystal surface is stable only above pH 14, which almost never occurs in water around living things. By about pH 10 each surface phosphate has gained one hydrogen and the hydroxide and some calcium have left. By about pH 5 each has gained two, and more calcium has gone. Near pH 7 the surface carries a mix, and an infrared measurement found 31% with one hydrogen and 69% with two.

When dry hydroxyapatite meets water it gives off heat, the immersion energy, measured in millijoules per square metre. Weighting the model faces by how much of a real crystal each one covers gives 619 mJ/m² at pH 7, and counting all faces equally gives 533. Heat measurements on perfectly dried crystals give 600 to 700. The comparison depends on how the faces are weighted and on how dry the real samples were, since a sample that has already taken up water from the air gives off less heat.
The slices are cut from the measured crystal structure, with hydrogens added and calcium removed by hand to show each step. They are illustrations, not simulation results.

slides.kicker: IFF Agent · The author’s described workflow
slides.title: The IFF Agent carries one material through eight steps
slides.lede: The IFF Agent is the author’s described workflow for building and checking an IFF model, one material at a time. Its first four steps decide what the result must show before anything is computed, including which measurements may tune the model and which are kept back as tests, so a test is never a number the model was tuned to.
slides.takeaway: The IFF Agent is a workflow around IFF, not part of the force field, and this presentation claims no results from it.
slides.alt: The eight steps of the IFF Agent drawn as pictures in two groups, each with rhodium’s published numbers. Set up, deciding what the result must show. 1 Ask, a rhodium surface in water. 2 Gather, papers and measured data for size, surface energy and stiffness. 3 Choose, a 12-6 pair curve marked with r₀ and ε. 4 Plan, rhodium’s cubic unit cell, tuning size and surface energy and keeping stiffness as a test. Run and check. 5 Fit, the curve tuned to r₀ = 2.757 Å and ε = 7.84 kcal/mol. 6 Test, bars of 209 GPa from IFF against 379 measured for stretching, 45% low. 7 Read back, the exported file gives −7.84 kcal/mol at r₀, not 0, with a tick. 8 Decide, a tick for surfaces and a red flag on stiffness. Every number comes from rhodium’s published values, and nothing here is a new fit or result.
notes: The IFF Agent is a workflow described by the author for building and checking IFF models step by step. It sits around the force field and is not part of it. This presentation describes the workflow only and claims no implementation or results from it.

Its eight steps are named intake, references, model, contract, run and fit, validate, export readback, and review and disposition. The first four decide what the result must show before anything is computed. The contract fixes in advance which measurements may be used for tuning and which are kept back as tests.

Rhodium shows the steps with the published numbers. The question is rhodium faces in water. The references are the measured size, surface energy and stiffness. The model is a 12-6 pair curve. The contract tunes the size and surface energy and keeps stiffness as a test. The fit gives r₀ = 2.757 Å and ε = 7.84 kcal/mol. The test finds a stretching stiffness of 209 GPa against 379 measured. The readback checks that the exported file gives −7.84 kcal/mol at r₀, not 0, which catches the mix-up between r₀ and σ described with the Lennard-Jones curve. The review approves the model for surfaces and flags its stiffness.
Every number comes from the 2021 rhodium paper, and none is a new fit or result.

slides.title: A flat ring on a triangular face explains the crystal shape
body: Swapping L for F shifted platinum crystals from cubes toward tetrahedra. In the simulations the F ring lies flat on triangular faces but not on square ones, so the triangular faces end up covering the crystal.

IFF puts metals, minerals, water and molecules into one model that is checked against experiments. With it, researchers can test on a computer which molecules stick to which surfaces before anything is made, from catalysts and medicine to bone and cement.
slides.alt: The S7 peptide on platinum in water again, with its phenylalanine ring highlighted where it lies flat on the surface.
notes: Back to the opening question. Swapping one amino acid, L for F, shifted platinum crystals from cubes toward tetrahedra. The simulations showed why. The F ring lies flat on the triangular face and sticks, while on the square face the ring stands up and the peptide does not stick. Crystals grow slowest on the faces that are covered, so the triangular faces end up covering the crystal, and a crystal with only triangular faces is a tetrahedron.

That answer needed all three sets of interactions in one model, which is what IFF provides. IFF supplies compatible interaction equations and material parameters so a classical simulation can describe a solid together with water, polymers or biological molecules. It addresses inconsistent material/surface descriptions and the difficulty of combining separately developed models, allowing supported interface structures, binding and energies to be calculated and compared with experiments.

The three examples each compared a different kind of result with experiment, the face a peptide prefers on platinum, how water wets silica, and the heat given off as water meets bone mineral. In each, it matters which measurements tuned the model and which were left to test it, and a standard model still cannot describe reactions.

Other published studies tested IFF in other ways. On silica, simulations with PCFF-SILICA, IFF’s silica model, compared the twelve-amino-acid peptide KSLSRHDHIHHH with two versions of it. In the experiments, swapping the histidine at position 6 for alanine made the peptide stick more, and the same swap at position 11, near the C-terminal end of the chain, made it stick less. The simulations ranked the three in the same order, but only on the surface model that matched the experiment, with about 4.7 OH groups per square nanometre. With twice as many, 9.4, the order changed.

For cement, Mishra, Flatt and Heinz computed the energy needed to pull two broken faces of tricalcium silicate apart at 90 °C, close to the conditions in a working mill. Bare faces needed 240 to 450 mJ/m², depending on whether water had reached them, and less than one layer of grinding additive cut that to between 50 and 110. These results are in section 4.3 and Figures 10 and 11 of their paper. Mill tests reported in a patent ranked three amine additives in the same order as the simulation. That is a ranking only, and glycerine, the fourth additive, was not in those tests.

For gold, a polarizable model, in which each gold atom’s electrons can shift towards or away from a nearby ion, gives −13.0 ± 0.1 kcal/mol per water molecule in a layer on gold’s triangular face, and the plain model −12.8 ± 0.1. Measurements on gold made of many small crystals give −13 and −15.5. The shift matters most for ions close to the metal, and for water the plain model is nearly as good.
Thank you. The notes for each slide hold the equations, the worked numbers and the sources behind it, and the reading version shows them with every slide.
